name: Structure
first: A type that groups values under one name, and whose instances are copied when they are assigned or passed to a function.

dependsOn.why: An instance of a structure is made by calling its initializer, which takes arguments after argument labels, as a function does.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `Trip(city: "Lima", nights: 3)` calls the initializer of `Trip` with two arguments, each after its argument label, as a call of a function does.

what.is: A structure is a type that groups values under one name. Each instance of a structure, one value of its type, holds its own copy of those values. Assigning an instance to a variable, or passing it to a function, copies it.
what.afterExample: `Trip` groups a city and a number of nights. Line 6 copies `first` into `second`, so when line 7 changes `second`, `first` still has 3 nights.
what.problem: Values that belong together, such as the city and the number of nights of one trip, are easier to use as one value. A structure gives them one name, so code passes one `Trip` instead of a separate `String` and `Int`.
what.how: Each instance holds a value for every stored property of the structure. Assigning the instance to another variable copies all of those values, so `first` and `second` are separate instances after line 6.

when.text: Use a structure for a group of values that should be copied, such as the details of a trip that a screen shows, so that changing one copy never changes another.
Don't use one when several parts of a program must share one instance and see each other's changes. A class does that: assigning an instance of a class copies only its address.

parts.name: The keyword `struct`, line 1
parts.text: The keyword `struct` declares a structure. The structure's name, `Trip`, comes right after it, and its stored properties are between the braces on lines 1 and 4.

parts.name: The stored properties, lines 2 and 3
parts.text: Lines 2 and 3 declare the stored properties of `Trip`: `city`, of type `String`, and `nights`, of type `Int`. Every instance of `Trip` holds its own value for each one. They are declared with `var`, so an instance in a variable can change them.

parts.name: The memberwise initializer, line 5
parts.text: An initializer is code that makes a new instance of a type. `Trip` declares none, so swiftc writes one for it, called the memberwise initializer. It has a parameter for each stored property, with the property's name as its argument label. Line 5 calls it with `"Lima"` and 3.

steps.text: Line 5 calls the memberwise initializer of `Trip`. It makes an instance whose `city` is `"Lima"` and whose `nights` is 3, and stores it in the constant `first`.
Line 6 copies the instance in `first`, and stores the copy in the variable `second`. There are now two instances of `Trip`, with the same values.
Line 7 sets `nights` of `second` to 5. Only the instance in `second` changes.
Line 8 prints the `nights` of `first`, which is still 3: {{3}}.

end.text: Each instance of a structure holds its own values. Line 6 made a copy, so the change on line 7 did not reach `first`.
